title: Yaa Asantewaa Leads the War of the Golden Stool
text:
In 1896 the British occupied Kumasi, capital of the Asante kingdom in what is now Ghana, and exiled its king, Prempeh I. Asante resentment grew. In March 1900 the British governor, Sir Frederick Hodgson, made a speech in Kumasi demanding to be given the Golden Stool so that he could sit on it.

The Golden Stool was the most sacred object of the Asante nation, believed to hold its soul. No one, not even the king, sat on it. The demand was an outrage.

The chiefs met in secret to discuss what to do. Yaa Asantewaa, the queen mother of Ejisu, was present. According to Asante oral tradition, when some of the men hesitated she told them that if they would not fight, the women would, and that she would call upon her fellow women.

The Asante rose. Under her leadership forces besieged the British in the Kumasi fort for months. British reinforcements eventually broke the siege, and Yaa Asantewaa was captured in 1901 and exiled to the Seychelles, where she died in 1921. The Golden Stool was never handed over, and the British did not demand it again.
lesson: When others hesitate, a leader who names what is at stake and steps forward first can give everyone the courage to act.
people: Yaa Asantewaa, Sir Frederick Hodgson, Prempeh I
source: British colonial records of the Asante war of 1900; Asante oral history
caveat: Her famous speech to the chiefs is known through oral tradition, and its exact words vary between versions.
